USER:
can you argue for the Catholic understanding of John 6?

ASSISTANT:
Certainly, I can provide an explanation of the Catholic understanding of John 6.

In John 6, Jesus speaks to a large crowd about the Bread of Life, saying, "I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will never be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty" (John 6:35, NRSV). He goes on to say, "Very truly, I tell you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you. Those who eat my flesh and drink my blood have eternal life, and I will raise them up on the last day" (John 6:53-54).

Catholics understand this passage to be referring to the Eucharist, which is the sacrament of the Body and Blood of Christ. They believe that Jesus is truly present, body, blood, soul, and divinity, in the Eucharist, and that when they receive Communion, they are receiving Jesus himself.

This belief is based on the words of Jesus at the Last Supper, when he said, "This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me" (Luke 22:19) and "This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood" (Luke 22:20). Catholics believe that Jesus was instituting the sacrament of the Eucharist at that moment, and that he meant his words to be taken literally.

The Catholic Church also looks to the early Church Fathers for support of this belief. For example, St. Ignatius of Antioch, who was a disciple of the apostle John, wrote in the early second century, "Take note of those who hold heterodox opinions on the grace of Jesus Christ which has come to us, and see how contrary their opinions are to the mind of God. [...] They abstain from the Eucharist and from prayer, because they do not confess that the Eucharist is the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ" (Letter to the Smyrneans, 6:2-7:1).

In summary, Catholics understand John 6 to be referring to the Eucharist, and believe that Jesus meant his words about eating his flesh and drinking his blood to be taken literally. They also look to the words of Jesus at the Last Supper and the writings of the early Church Fathers as evidence for this belief.

USER:
why do they believe he would literally want people to consume his physical body? doesn't this go against the jewish laws?

ASSISTANT:
Catholics believe that Jesus intended for his followers to consume his physical body in the form of the Eucharist, not as a violation of Jewish law, but as a fulfillment of it. They believe that Jesus, as a Jew, was well-versed in the Jewish scriptures and tradition, and that he was intimately familiar with the Passover feast.

During the Passover, the Jews would celebrate the Exodus from Egypt by sacrificing a lamb and eating its flesh. This sacrifice and consumption of the lamb was a symbol of the covenant between God and his people. Jesus, at the Last Supper, transformed this ritual into a new covenant by offering himself as the true Lamb of God, whose flesh and blood would be given for the salvation of all people.

Furthermore, Catholics believe that Jesus is not merely a human being, but is also the Son of God. As such, they believe that Jesus has the power to transform bread and wine into his own body and blood. This belief is based on the words of Jesus himself when he said, "This is my body" and "This cup is the new covenant in my blood" (Luke 22:19-20). Catholics interpret these words as a literal statement of fact, rather than a metaphorical or symbolic statement.

While it may seem to go against Jewish laws and traditions to consume human flesh and blood, Catholics believe that Jesus was offering himself as a spiritual nourishment, rather than a physical one. They do not believe that the Eucharist is cannibalistic, but rather a participation in the sacrifice of Christ, who gave his body and blood for the salvation of all humanity.

USER:

ASSISTANT:
The Catholic Church believes that the consumption of the Eucharist is not cannibalistic because the reality of what is being consumed is not the physical body and blood of Jesus, but the glorified and risen Christ under the appearance of bread and wine. Catholics believe that the substance or essence of the bread and wine is transformed into the substance or essence of the body and blood of Christ, while the accidents or appearances of bread and wine remain.

This belief is based on the doctrine of transubstantiation, which holds that at the moment of consecration during the Mass, the entire substance of the bread and wine is changed into the substance of Christ's body and blood, while the accidents or appearances of bread and wine remain. Therefore, Catholics believe that when they receive the Eucharist, they are receiving the true and real presence of Christ, but not in a cannibalistic sense because they are not consuming human flesh and blood.

Catholics believe that this transformation of the bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ is a mystery that cannot be fully understood or explained by human reason alone. They believe that it is a divine mystery that requires faith to accept and believe.

In summary, while the consumption of the Eucharist may seem to involve the consumption of human flesh and blood, Catholics believe that it is not cannibalistic because what is being consumed is not the physical body and blood of Jesus, but the glorified and risen Christ under the appearance of bread and wine. This belief is based on the doctrine of transubstantiation and the understanding that the substance of the bread and wine is transformed into the substance of Christ's body and blood while the accidents or appearances of bread and wine remain.

USER:
wouldn't Christ's glorified self still be human though? when we rise from the dead, do we still have human qualities?

ASSISTANT:
Yes, Catholics believe that even in his glorified state, Jesus remains fully human and fully divine. The Catechism of the Catholic Church teaches that at the Resurrection, Jesus' body was transformed and glorified, and that this transformation was a sign of his divine glory and power (CCC 659-660).

Furthermore, Catholics believe that at the general Resurrection, all people will be raised with glorified bodies that are transformed and perfected. While the nature of these glorified bodies is a mystery, Catholics believe that they will retain their essential human qualities, while being freed from the limitations and imperfections of the earthly body.

Catholics believe that the glorified body will be spiritual, incorruptible, and immortal, and that it will be a reflection of the glory of God. The glorified body will also be perfectly united to the soul, and will be free from any suffering or imperfection.

In summary, Catholics believe that even in his glorified state, Jesus remains fully human and fully divine. Catholics also believe that at the general Resurrection, all people will be raised with glorified bodies that retain their essential human qualities, but are transformed and perfected in a spiritual and immortal way.

USER:

ASSISTANT:
Catholics believe that the Eucharist is not cannibalistic because, although Jesus remains fully human in his glorified state, he is not physically present in the Eucharist in the same way as he was when he lived on earth. Rather, Catholics believe that the Eucharist is a sacrament in which the substance or essence of bread and wine are transformed into the substance or essence of the body and blood of Christ, while the physical properties or "accidents" of bread and wine remain.

This transformation of the bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ is known as transubstantiation, and it is considered a mystery that cannot be fully comprehended by human reason. Catholics believe that the Eucharist is a participation in the sacrificial death of Christ, and that through it, they receive the real and substantial presence of Christ.

Although the Eucharist involves the consumption of bread and wine, Catholics believe that it is not cannibalistic because the substance of the bread and wine has been changed into the substance of Christ's body and blood, while the physical properties or "accidents" of bread and wine remain. Therefore, Catholics do not believe that they are consuming human flesh and blood, but rather the true and real presence of Christ in the Eucharist.

USER:

When Catholics say that the Eucharist contains the essence of the body and blood of Christ, they mean that the substance or essence of the bread and wine has been changed into the substance or essence of Christ's body and blood. This transformation is understood as a sacramental reality, in which the appearances or "accidents" of bread and wine remain, but the substance or essence of the bread and wine has been transformed into the substance or essence of Christ's body and blood.

However, Catholics do not believe that the Eucharist is simply a symbolic or metaphorical representation of Christ's body and blood, but rather that it is a real and substantial participation in the sacrifice of Christ. In summary, when Catholics say that the Eucharist contains the essence of the body and blood of Christ, they mean that the substance or essence of the bread and wine has been transformed into the substance or essence of Christ's body and blood through transubstantiation. Although the appearances or "accidents" of bread and wine remain, the true and real presence of Christ is received by the faithful in the sacrament of the Eucharist.
